City of Merri Creek Library Service
Program Report — Summer Reading Club 2024-25
Report date: 15 March 2025
Period covered: 1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025
Prepared by: Community Programs Team
Approved for release: 20 March 2025

---

1. Introduction

The Summer Reading Club 2024-25 ran across all four branches of the City of Merri Creek Library Service (Merri Creek Central, Eastgate, Riverside, and Northwood) from Sunday 1 December 2024 through to Friday 28 February 2025. The program is an annual fixture in the library service calendar, aimed at maintaining and strengthening reading habits among children and young people during the summer holiday period. It is delivered in partnership with local schools, the Merri Creek Community Centre, and the statewide public library network.

This report summarises participation, program delivery, partner involvement, and key outcomes for the 2024-25 season. It also records learnings that will inform planning for the 2025-26 program.

2. Participation

2.1 Registration and attendance

Total registrations for Summer Reading Club 2024-25 were 342 participants. This figure is historical and reflects the final confirmed registration total as at program close on 28 February 2025. Summer Reading Club 2024-25 had a participant_count of 342 participants. Record status: historical.

Registrations were lower than the 2023-24 season, which recorded 371 registrations. The decline of 29 participants (approximately 8%) is attributed in part to the timing of the summer school holidays, which began later than in previous years, and to competition from a newly introduced council-run holiday sports program. Registration numbers were nonetheless in line with the five-year average of 348.

Table 1 below shows registrations by branch and age group.

Table 1: Registrations by branch and age group, SRC 2024-25

| Branch | 0-5 years | 6-8 years | 9-12 years | 13-17 years | Total |
|---------------------|-----------|-----------|------------|-------------|-------|
| Merri Creek Central | 22 | 48 | 41 | 12 | 123 |
| Eastgate | 18 | 35 | 29 | 9 | 91 |
| Riverside | 14 | 27 | 22 | 5 | 68 |
| Northwood | 11 | 26 | 18 | 5 | 60 |
| **Total** | **65** | **136** | **110** | **31** | **342** |

Age group data was collected at the point of registration. The 6-8 years group was the largest cohort (136 participants, 40% of total registrations), consistent with previous years. The 13-17 years group remained the smallest cohort (31 participants, 9%), and this continues to be an area of focus for future program design.

2.2 Completion

Of the 342 registered participants, 229 completed the program requirements (reading at least 12 books or equivalent and submitting a completion form at a branch). This represents a completion rate of 67%. The completion rate for 2023-24 was 71%.

The reduction in completion rate is consistent with the overall drop in registrations and with feedback from families about competing holiday activities. Completion rates were highest at Riverside (72%) and lowest at Northwood (61%). A breakdown of completion by branch is provided in Table 2.

Table 2: Completion by branch, SRC 2024-25

| Branch | Registrations | Completed | Completion rate |
|---------------------|---------------|-----------|-----------------|
| Merri Creek Central | 123 | 82 | 67% |
| Eastgate | 91 | 61 | 67% |
| Riverside | 68 | 49 | 72% |
| Northwood | 60 | 37 | 61% |
| **Total** | **342** | **229** | **67%** |

2.3 Participation at events

In addition to the reading challenge itself, the Summer Reading Club included 14 in-branch events and 6 outreach sessions. Total attendance at these events was 486, including siblings and accompanying adults. Highlights included:

- Author visit with local children's author Mia Trantham at Merri Creek Central (attendance: 54)
- Wildlife incursion with the Merri Creek Catchment Group at Eastgate (attendance: 62)
- Craft and storytelling mornings at all four branches (combined attendance: 198)
- A dedicated teen book club session at Northwood (attendance: 14)
Twenty-three registered participants (7%) were identified as having a disability or additional learning support need at the time of registration. Of these, 14 completed the program, giving a completion rate of 61% for this group. Feedback from parents and carers indicated that the completion form was difficult for some children to use independently, particularly for younger participants and those with literacy difficulties. Staff trialled a verbal completion option at Merri Creek Central and Eastgate; this was well received and will be considered for all branches in 2025-26.

Seven families requested modified program materials, including large-print reading logs and additional time to complete the challenge. All requests were accommodated.

**Geographic spread**

Registrations were mapped to postcodes at the time of registration. The majority of participants (221, or 65%) resided within the City of Merri Creek local government area. A further 87 (25%) resided in neighbouring LGAs and 34 (10%) were visiting the area during the summer holiday period. The visiting cohort was higher than in previous years, which staff attribute to the program being listed on the Visit Victoria school holiday website for the first time.

## 2.5 Participant feedback

Feedback was collected via a short survey distributed at completion, and via an online form sent to all registered families in the final week of the program. A total of 176 responses were received (51% of registered families). In addition, 34 informal comments were recorded by branch staff during the program and are included below where relevant.

**Survey results**

| Question | Strongly agree / agree | Neutral | Disagree / strongly disagree |
|---|---|---|---|
| My child enjoyed the Summer Reading Club | 84% | 11% | 5% |
| The reading log was easy to use | 62% | 21% | 17% |
| The prize collection process was straightforward | 71% | 18% | 11% |
| My child was motivated to read more than usual | 78% | 14% | 8% |
| I would recommend the program to other families | 81% | 12% | 7% |

The most common suggestion in open-ended responses was for more event sessions, particularly on weekends and during the final two weeks of January when many families reported having "run out of things to do". Eighteen responses mentioned the desire for a longer program or an extension into March. Twelve responses requested more diverse book recommendations, including graphic novels and non-fiction titles.

Selected written comments from the survey:

Summer Reading Club 2024-25 completion_rate_percent was 67 percent. Record status: historical.

> "My daughter loved the wildlife incursion and has been talking about it for weeks. She read twice as many books as she needed to. No worries at all, great program."

> "Good value for a free program. The staff at Eastgate were lovely and very patient with my son who has autism. The verbal completion option made a big difference for him."

> "The reading log is a bit fiddly for younger kids. My 6 year old needed help every time. Maybe a sticker chart version for the littlies?"

> "We are a visiting family from Perth and found the program by accident. It was a highlight of our holiday. Would love to see something similar at home."

> "The prizes were fine but my child was disappointed that the book voucher could only be used at the library bookshop. She wanted to choose something from a regular bookshop."

> "More teen-focused events please. My 14 year old attended the book club at Northwood and enjoyed it, but there was only the one session."

Informal comments recorded by staff included praise for the craft mornings ("the best thing we did all summer" - parent, Riverside), a request for bilingual reading logs, and several comments about the heat in the Northwood meeting room during the January sessions.

## 2.6 Prize distribution

Prizes were funded through the program budget and through a partnership with the Friends of Merri Creek Library group. All 229 participants who completed the program received a completion certificate and a small prize pack. Prize packs included a book voucher (value $10), a bookmark, and a temporary tattoo featuring the program mascot, Wombat Wayne.
## 3. Budget Summary

The Summer Reading Club 2024-25 was delivered within its approved budget of $18,500. A summary of expenditure against budget is provided below. All figures are GST-inclusive and have been rounded to the nearest whole dollar. The program was funded from the Library Service's community programs allocation, with additional in-kind support from the Friends of Merri Creek Library group and the Eastgate Shopping Centre management.

**Table 3.1: Program Budget vs Actual Expenditure (01/12/2024 – 28/02/2025)**

| Item | Budget ($) | Actual ($) | Variance ($) | Notes |
|------|------------|------------|--------------|-------|
| Staffing (casual program officers, 3 branches) | 7,500 | 7,860 | -360 | Additional shifts for Northwood January heat-relocation sessions |
| Honoraria (guest presenters, incursions) | 2,800 | 2,750 | +50 | Wildlife incursion came in under quote |
| Materials (reading logs, certificates, bookmarks) | 2,400 | 2,310 | +90 | Bulk printing discount from Merri Print Co. |
| Prizes (book vouchers, temporary tattoos, misc.) | 3,200 | 3,410 | -210 | Voucher value held at $10 per completer; uptake slightly above forecast |
| Marketing (posters, social media boost, flyers) | 1,200 | 1,180 | +20 | Facebook boost under-spent; flyer printing as planned |
| Venue hire / room bookings (Eastgate pop-up) | 800 | 640 | +160 | One session cancelled due to heat |
| Refreshments (craft mornings, teen book club) | 600 | 545 | +55 | Tea, coffee, juice and biscuits; volunteer-supplied baking reduced cost |
| Contingency | 0 | 0 | 0 | Not required |
| **Total** | **18,500** | **18,695** | **-195** | |

The over-expenditure of $195 was absorbed within the Library Service's minor variance threshold (up to 2% of program budget) and did not require a supplementary budget request. The largest single variance was in prizes, driven by a final completion rate slightly above the planning assumption of 220 completers. The final completion rate was 67 percent. This has been recorded as historical data in the program evaluation system, noting that the 2024-25 figure sits below the five-year average of 71 percent but above the 2022-23 result of 61 percent.

## 4. Volunteer Hours

Volunteers contributed a total of 214.5 hours to the Summer Reading Club across the three branches (Eastgate, Northwood, and Riverside) and the Eastgate pop-up space. Hours are recorded in half-hour increments and include preparation time, session support, and post-program pack-down. Volunteer hours were not costed in the budget above, as they are treated as in-kind community contribution.

**Table 4.1: Volunteer Hours by Branch and Activity (01/12/2024 – 28/02/2025)**

| Branch / Location | Preparation | Session Support | Pack-down | Total Hours |
|-------------------|-------------|-----------------|-----------|-------------|
| Eastgate | 18.5 | 41.0 | 6.5 | 66.0 |
| Northwood | 15.0 | 38.5 | 5.0 | 58.5 |

Volunteer hours peaked in January (89.5 hours) during the school holiday period, with a secondary peak in the final week of February as families returned logs and collected prizes. The volunteer team comprised 14 regular volunteers from the Library's established volunteer pool, plus 4 short-term volunteers recruited specifically for the program through the Council's volunteer portal. All volunteers completed the standard library induction and a program-specific briefing session held on 28 November 2024.

One volunteer, Margaret H., contributed 28.5 hours across all three branches, assisting primarily with prize pack assembly and the craft mornings. Her contribution was acknowledged at the volunteer appreciation afternoon tea held on 12 March 2025.

City of Merri Creek Library Service
Digital Skills Survey 2025 – Results Summary
Compiled: 10/05/2025
Prepared by: Community Programs Team

1. Background

The Digital Skills Survey 2025 was conducted to collect feedback and self-reported skill levels from participants in the Library Service's digital literacy programs. The survey was distributed in both print and online formats, and was open from 15/03/2025 to 30/04/2025. This summary presents the compiled results for use by program evaluators and coordinators.

2. Methodology

The survey comprised 14 questions covering:

- Demographic information (age group, gender, postcode)
- Frequency of library digital program attendance
- Self-assessed skill levels across five areas (using a 1–5 scale)
- Overall satisfaction with programs (1–5 scale)
- Open-ended comments and suggestions

Surveys were offered at the end of sessions and via a link distributed in the Library's e-news and on the website. No incentives were offered. Participation was voluntary and anonymous.

Response rate: The survey was distributed to all program attendees during the survey period. Attendance records for the period show approximately 410 individual attendances (including repeat attendees). The survey received 128 responses. Digital Skills Survey 2025 survey_response_count was 128 responses. Record status: current. This represents a response rate of approximately 31% of total attendances, noting that some respondents may have attended more than one session.

3. Response Summary

All 128 responses were included in the analysis. 121 responses were submitted online; 7 were completed on paper and entered manually by staff. Two paper forms were partially completed and have been included with missing data noted.

9. Confidence Improvement

Respondents were asked whether they felt more confident using digital technology after attending programs. Overall, 34 percent of respondents reported an improvement in confidence. Respondents were asked to select which aspects of the programs helped them most. They could select more than one option.

Respondents who attended fewer than three sessions were asked what made it difficult to attend more. Common responses are summarised below.

Open-ended suggestions were grouped into common themes. The most frequently mentioned themes are listed below.

| Theme | Number of mentions |
|---|---|
| More sessions on myGov and Medicare | 22 |
| Follow-up sessions after the course | 18 |
| Evening or weekend classes | 15 |

| One-on-one help available | 8 |

A further selection of comments is provided below. Comments have been lightly edited for legibility but not for content.

- "I had never used a computer before. Now I can email my grandchildren."
- "The handouts are great, I keep them by the computer at home."
- "More classes please, especially for seniors."
- "The tutor made everyone feel welcome, even if we were slow."
- "I would like to learn how to pay bills online."
- "Good value and friendly atmosphere. Thanks to the library."
- "Could the classes be a bit longer? We always ran out of time."
- "I liked that we could practice on our own devices."

15. Recommendations

Based on the survey results, the following recommendations are proposed for the next program cycle:

1. Continue offering introductory sessions, as demand remains strong and satisfaction is high.
2. Develop a short follow-up session (4–6 weeks after the main course) to reinforce skills, as requested by 18 respondents.
3. Add at least one evening or weekend class per term to address timing barriers.
4. Expand content on myGov and Medicare, given the number of requests.
5. Produce a simple practice sheet for each topic so participants can continue at home.
6. Consider a short session on online banking and payments, as several respondents expressed interest.
7. Investigate options for childcare during weekday morning sessions, where feasible.

16. Next Steps

The full dataset and individual responses are stored on the shared drive under Digital Skills Survey 2025 – Responses.xlsx. Raw comments are in the tab labelled Open Ended. The survey will be repeated in September 2025, with a similar format to allow comparison over time.

documents.title: Summer Reading Club 2024-25 Final Report
documents.content:
City of Merri Creek Library Service
Program Report — Summer Reading Club 2024-25
Report date: 15 March 2025
Period covered: 1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025
Prepared by: Community Programs Team
Approved for release: 20 March 2025

---

1. Introduction

The Summer Reading Club 2024-25 ran across all four branches of the City of Merri Creek Library Service (Merri Creek Central, Eastgate, Riverside, and Northwood) from Sunday 1 December 2024 through to Friday 28 February 2025. The program is an annual fixture in the library service calendar, aimed at maintaining and strengthening reading habits among children and young people during the summer holiday period. It is delivered in partnership with local schools, the Merri Creek Community Centre, and the statewide public library network.

This report summarises participation, program delivery, partner involvement, and key outcomes for the 2024-25 season. It also records learnings that will inform planning for the 2025-26 program.

2. Participation

2.1 Registration and attendance

Total registrations for Summer Reading Club 2024-25 were 342 participants. This figure is historical and reflects the final confirmed registration total as at program close on 28 February 2025. Summer Reading Club 2024-25 had a participant_count of 342 participants. Record status: historical.

Registrations were lower than the 2023-24 season, which recorded 371 registrations. The decline of 29 participants (approximately 8%) is attributed in part to the timing of the summer school holidays, which began later than in previous years, and to competition from a newly introduced council-run holiday sports program. Registration numbers were nonetheless in line with the five-year average of 348.

Table 1 below shows registrations by branch and age group.

Table 1: Registrations by branch and age group, SRC 2024-25

| Branch | 0-5 years | 6-8 years | 9-12 years | 13-17 years | Total |
|---------------------|-----------|-----------|------------|-------------|-------|
| Merri Creek Central | 22 | 48 | 41 | 12 | 123 |
| Eastgate | 18 | 35 | 29 | 9 | 91 |
| Riverside | 14 | 27 | 22 | 5 | 68 |
| Northwood | 11 | 26 | 18 | 5 | 60 |
| **Total** | **65** | **136** | **110** | **31** | **342** |

Age group data was collected at the point of registration. The 6-8 years group was the largest cohort (136 participants, 40% of total registrations), consistent with previous years. The 13-17 years group remained the smallest cohort (31 participants, 9%), and this continues to be an area of focus for future program design.

2.2 Completion

Of the 342 registered participants, 229 completed the program requirements (reading at least 12 books or equivalent and submitting a completion form at a branch). This represents a completion rate of 67%. The completion rate for 2023-24 was 71%.

The reduction in completion rate is consistent with the overall drop in registrations and with feedback from families about competing holiday activities. Completion rates were highest at Riverside (72%) and lowest at Northwood (61%). A breakdown of completion by branch is provided in Table 2.

Table 2: Completion by branch, SRC 2024-25

| Branch | Registrations | Completed | Completion rate |
|---------------------|---------------|-----------|-----------------|
| Merri Creek Central | 123 | 82 | 67% |
| Eastgate | 91 | 61 | 67% |
| Riverside | 68 | 49 | 72% |
| Northwood | 60 | 37 | 61% |
| **Total** | **342** | **229** | **67%** |

2.3 Participation at events

In addition to the reading challenge itself, the Summer Reading Club included 14 in-branch events and 6 outreach sessions. Total attendance at these events was 486, including siblings and accompanying adults. Highlights included:

- Author visit with local children's author Mia Trantham at Merri Creek Central (attendance: 54)
- Wildlife incursion with the Merri Creek Catchment Group at Eastgate (attendance: 62)
- Craft and storytelling mornings at all four branches (combined attendance: 198)
- A dedicated teen book club session at Northwood (attendance: 14)

documents.title: Summer Reading Club 2024-25 Final Report
documents.content:
Twenty-three registered participants (7%) were identified as having a disability or additional learning support need at the time of registration. Of these, 14 completed the program, giving a completion rate of 61% for this group. Feedback from parents and carers indicated that the completion form was difficult for some children to use independently, particularly for younger participants and those with literacy difficulties. Staff trialled a verbal completion option at Merri Creek Central and Eastgate; this was well received and will be considered for all branches in 2025-26.

Seven families requested modified program materials, including large-print reading logs and additional time to complete the challenge. All requests were accommodated.

**Geographic spread**

Registrations were mapped to postcodes at the time of registration. The majority of participants (221, or 65%) resided within the City of Merri Creek local government area. A further 87 (25%) resided in neighbouring LGAs and 34 (10%) were visiting the area during the summer holiday period. The visiting cohort was higher than in previous years, which staff attribute to the program being listed on the Visit Victoria school holiday website for the first time.

## 2.5 Participant feedback

Feedback was collected via a short survey distributed at completion, and via an online form sent to all registered families in the final week of the program. A total of 176 responses were received (51% of registered families). In addition, 34 informal comments were recorded by branch staff during the program and are included below where relevant.

**Survey results**

| Question | Strongly agree / agree | Neutral | Disagree / strongly disagree |
|---|---|---|---|
| My child enjoyed the Summer Reading Club | 84% | 11% | 5% |
| The reading log was easy to use | 62% | 21% | 17% |
| The prize collection process was straightforward | 71% | 18% | 11% |
| My child was motivated to read more than usual | 78% | 14% | 8% |
| I would recommend the program to other families | 81% | 12% | 7% |

The most common suggestion in open-ended responses was for more event sessions, particularly on weekends and during the final two weeks of January when many families reported having "run out of things to do". Eighteen responses mentioned the desire for a longer program or an extension into March. Twelve responses requested more diverse book recommendations, including graphic novels and non-fiction titles.

Selected written comments from the survey:

Summer Reading Club 2024-25 completion_rate_percent was 67 percent. Record status: historical.

> "My daughter loved the wildlife incursion and has been talking about it for weeks. She read twice as many books as she needed to. No worries at all, great program."

> "Good value for a free program. The staff at Eastgate were lovely and very patient with my son who has autism. The verbal completion option made a big difference for him."

> "The reading log is a bit fiddly for younger kids. My 6 year old needed help every time. Maybe a sticker chart version for the littlies?"

> "We are a visiting family from Perth and found the program by accident. It was a highlight of our holiday. Would love to see something similar at home."

> "The prizes were fine but my child was disappointed that the book voucher could only be used at the library bookshop. She wanted to choose something from a regular bookshop."

> "More teen-focused events please. My 14 year old attended the book club at Northwood and enjoyed it, but there was only the one session."

Informal comments recorded by staff included praise for the craft mornings ("the best thing we did all summer" - parent, Riverside), a request for bilingual reading logs, and several comments about the heat in the Northwood meeting room during the January sessions.

## 2.6 Prize distribution

Prizes were funded through the program budget and through a partnership with the Friends of Merri Creek Library group. All 229 participants who completed the program received a completion certificate and a small prize pack. Prize packs included a book voucher (value $10), a bookmark, and a temporary tattoo featuring the program mascot, Wombat Wayne.

## 3. Budget Summary

The Summer Reading Club 2024-25 was delivered within its approved budget of $18,500. A summary of expenditure against budget is provided below. All figures are GST-inclusive and have been rounded to the nearest whole dollar. The program was funded from the Library Service's community programs allocation, with additional in-kind support from the Friends of Merri Creek Library group and the Eastgate Shopping Centre management.

**Table 3.1: Program Budget vs Actual Expenditure (01/12/2024 – 28/02/2025)**

| Item | Budget ($) | Actual ($) | Variance ($) | Notes |
|------|------------|------------|--------------|-------|
| Staffing (casual program officers, 3 branches) | 7,500 | 7,860 | -360 | Additional shifts for Northwood January heat-relocation sessions |
| Honoraria (guest presenters, incursions) | 2,800 | 2,750 | +50 | Wildlife incursion came in under quote |
| Materials (reading logs, certificates, bookmarks) | 2,400 | 2,310 | +90 | Bulk printing discount from Merri Print Co. |
| Prizes (book vouchers, temporary tattoos, misc.) | 3,200 | 3,410 | -210 | Voucher value held at $10 per completer; uptake slightly above forecast |
| Marketing (posters, social media boost, flyers) | 1,200 | 1,180 | +20 | Facebook boost under-spent; flyer printing as planned |
| Venue hire / room bookings (Eastgate pop-up) | 800 | 640 | +160 | One session cancelled due to heat |
| Refreshments (craft mornings, teen book club) | 600 | 545 | +55 | Tea, coffee, juice and biscuits; volunteer-supplied baking reduced cost |
| Contingency | 0 | 0 | 0 | Not required |
| **Total** | **18,500** | **18,695** | **-195** | |

The over-expenditure of $195 was absorbed within the Library Service's minor variance threshold (up to 2% of program budget) and did not require a supplementary budget request. The largest single variance was in prizes, driven by a final completion rate slightly above the planning assumption of 220 completers. The final completion rate was 67 percent. This has been recorded as historical data in the program evaluation system, noting that the 2024-25 figure sits below the five-year average of 71 percent but above the 2022-23 result of 61 percent.

## 4. Volunteer Hours

Volunteers contributed a total of 214.5 hours to the Summer Reading Club across the three branches (Eastgate, Northwood, and Riverside) and the Eastgate pop-up space. Hours are recorded in half-hour increments and include preparation time, session support, and post-program pack-down. Volunteer hours were not costed in the budget above, as they are treated as in-kind community contribution.

**Table 4.1: Volunteer Hours by Branch and Activity (01/12/2024 – 28/02/2025)**

| Branch / Location | Preparation | Session Support | Pack-down | Total Hours |
|-------------------|-------------|-----------------|-----------|-------------|
| Eastgate | 18.5 | 41.0 | 6.5 | 66.0 |
| Northwood | 15.0 | 38.5 | 5.0 | 58.5 |

Volunteer hours peaked in January (89.5 hours) during the school holiday period, with a secondary peak in the final week of February as families returned logs and collected prizes. The volunteer team comprised 14 regular volunteers from the Library's established volunteer pool, plus 4 short-term volunteers recruited specifically for the program through the Council's volunteer portal. All volunteers completed the standard library induction and a program-specific briefing session held on 28 November 2024.

One volunteer, Margaret H., contributed 28.5 hours across all three branches, assisting primarily with prize pack assembly and the craft mornings. Her contribution was acknowledged at the volunteer appreciation afternoon tea held on 12 March 2025.

City of Merri Creek Library Service
Digital Skills Survey 2025 – Results Summary
Compiled: 10/05/2025
Prepared by: Community Programs Team

---

1. Background

The Digital Skills Survey 2025 was conducted to collect feedback and self-reported skill levels from participants in the Library Service's digital literacy programs. The survey was distributed in both print and online formats, and was open from 15/03/2025 to 30/04/2025. This summary presents the compiled results for use by program evaluators and coordinators.

2. Methodology

The survey comprised 14 questions covering:

- Demographic information (age group, gender, postcode)
- Frequency of library digital program attendance
- Self-assessed skill levels across five areas (using a 1–5 scale)
- Overall satisfaction with programs (1–5 scale)
- Open-ended comments and suggestions

documents.content:
9. Confidence Improvement

Respondents were asked whether they felt more confident using digital technology after attending programs. Overall, 34 percent of respondents reported an improvement in confidence. Digital Skills Survey 2025 confidence_improvement_percent was 34 percent. Record status: current. This figure is current and reflects responses collected during the survey period.

When broken down by number of sessions attended, confidence improvement varied:

| Sessions attended | Reported confidence improvement |
|---|---|
| 1 session | 21% |
| 2–3 sessions | 33% |
| 4–6 sessions | 41% |
| 7 or more sessions | 52% |

A small number of respondents (4) did not answer this question. Their responses were excluded from the percentage calculation.

10. Skill Gains by Program Type

Respondents were asked to identify which programs they had attended and to rate their skill improvement in each area. The table below shows the percentage of respondents who reported a gain of at least one point on the 1–5 scale.

| Program type | Respondents attending | Reported skill gain |
|---|---|---|
| Email basics | 38 | 74% |
| Internet searching | 35 | 69% |
| Online safety | 41 | 78% |
| Smartphone/tablet apps | 29 | 66% |
| Online forms and government services | 33 | 71% |

Note: respondents could attend more than one program type, so numbers do not add to 128.

11. What Helped Most

Respondents were asked to select which aspects of the programs helped them most. They could select more than one option.

| Aspect | Number of selections |
|---|---|
| Patient tutor | 89 |
| Hands-on practice | 76 |
| Small class size | 64 |
| Printed handouts to take home | 52 |
| Being able to ask questions at my own pace | 48 |
| Peer support from other learners | 31 |

12. Barriers to Attendance

Respondents who attended fewer than three sessions were asked what made it difficult to attend more. Common responses are summarised below.

Note: respondents could list more than one barrier. 26 respondents in this group did not provide an answer.

13. Suggestions for Future Programs

Open-ended suggestions were grouped into common themes. The most frequently mentioned themes are listed below.

| Theme | Number of mentions |
|---|---|
| More sessions on myGov and Medicare | 22 |
| Follow-up sessions after the course | 18 |
| Evening or weekend classes | 15 |
| More advanced topics (e.g., online banking) | 12 |
| Longer sessions | 9 |
| One-on-one help available | 8 |
| Classes in other languages | 6 |

14. Additional Comments

A further selection of comments is provided below. Comments have been lightly edited for legibility but not for content.

- "I had never used a computer before. Now I can email my grandchildren."
- "The handouts are great, I keep them by the computer at home."
- "More classes please, especially for seniors."
- "The tutor made everyone feel welcome, even if we were slow."
- "I would like to learn how to pay bills online."
- "Good value and friendly atmosphere. Thanks to the library."
- "Could the classes be a bit longer? We always ran out of time."
- "I liked that we could practice on our own devices."

15. Recommendations

Based on the survey results, the following recommendations are proposed for the next program cycle:

1. Continue offering introductory sessions, as demand remains strong and satisfaction is high.
2. Develop a short follow-up session (4–6 weeks after the main course) to reinforce skills, as requested by 18 respondents.
3. Add at least one evening or weekend class per term to address timing barriers.
4. Expand content on myGov and Medicare, given the number of requests.
5. Produce a simple practice sheet for each topic so participants can continue at home.
6. Consider a short session on online banking and payments, as several respondents expressed interest.
7. Investigate options for childcare during weekday morning sessions, where feasible.

16. Next Steps

The full dataset and individual responses are stored on the shared drive under Digital Skills Survey 2025 – Responses.xlsx. Raw comments are in the tab labelled Open Ended. The survey will be repeated in September 2025, with a similar format to allow comparison over time.
